opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really one of the key things we've been focused on at SambaNova. If you look at how enterprises actually want to use AI, it's not one giant model that does everything. What they want is lots of models — many of them fine-tuned or specialized for particular tasks, particular domains, maybe particular customers or departments. You might have a model that's really good at SQL generation, another one tuned for legal documents, another one for customer support in a specific language, and so on.

The problem with conventional GPU-based systems is that the high-bandwidth memory is fast but quite limited in capacity. So if you want to serve a model, you basically have to keep it resident in HBM, and if you want to serve many models, you need many systems, or you end up swapping models in and out from host memory, which is very slow. That switching cost kills your latency and your utilization.

What we did with our architecture is build a three-tier memory system. We've got on-chip SRAM, which is very fast and lets us do the dataflow execution and fuse operations together. Then we have HBM, and then a large-capacity DRAM tier sitting right next to the accelerator. That big DRAM tier means you can hold hundreds of models — or a huge number of fine-tuned experts — on a single node, and then move the one you need into HBM very quickly, on the order of milliseconds, rather than going all the way back to the host.

That enables what we call a "composition of experts" approach. Instead of one monolithic trillion-parameter model, you can have a collection of smaller expert models plus a router that picks which expert should handle a given request. You get the capability of a very large model in aggregate, but each individual inference only runs a smaller model, so it's much more efficient. And it's also much easier to manage: if you want to update one expert, add a new one, or control access so certain users only see certain models, you can do that without retraining some giant model.

And this becomes even more important with agentic workflows. When you have agents chaining together many calls, often to different models — a planner, a coder, a verifier, a retrieval model — you really want to be able to hop between those models with very low latency. If every switch costs you seconds, the whole pipeline becomes unusable. With high-capacity memory close to the compute, the switching cost becomes negligible, so you can serve all of that from a much smaller footprint, which is a big win in terms of cost, power, and the number of racks you need in the data center.

r001.rationale: The response says nearby DRAM lets models move into HBM quickly and contrasts this with going back to host memory, but it does not attribute the speed to higher bandwidth than a host connection over PCIe.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So one of the things we've seen as models have gotten deployed more broadly is that the number of models people actually want to serve keeps multiplying. You might have one base model, but then you have dozens or hundreds of fine-tuned variants for different customers, different tasks, different languages. And if your accelerator only has a modest amount of on-device memory, you end up swapping those models in and out all the time. You're paying the cost of pulling weights over the interconnect from host memory or over the network, and that completely dominates your latency and wrecks your utilization.

With the SambaNova architecture, we deliberately built in a very large memory capacity, terabytes per node rather than the tens of gigabytes you'd see on a conventional GPU. The advantage is that you can keep all of those models resident at once. So when a request comes in for model A and the next one is for model B, there's no reload; you just switch, and that switch is essentially instantaneous from the application's point of view. You get the serving density of a single system handling many customers without the "cold start" penalty every time the workload mix changes.

The other piece is that this plays very well with how enterprises actually use these models. They don't want one giant model for everything; they want a model that's been adapted on their data, and they want to keep that private. High-capacity memory lets you host a whole fleet of those custom models economically, with good latency, on a relatively small footprint. And as context lengths grow and KV caches get bigger, that headroom just becomes more valuable, because it's not only the weights you're holding, it's all the intermediate state for the active requests too.

r001.rationale: The response says resident models can be switched without reloading, but does not attribute that low latency to higher bandwidth than a host connection over PCIe.

astra-6.text: The advantage is that you can keep a large number of custom models resident in memory. As requests come in, you can direct them to the appropriate model without first loading its weights from somewhere else. That reduces latency, especially when you’re switching among models for different users or applications. So you can share the inference infrastructure across many customized models while keeping it responsive, rather than dedicating a separate system to each one.

r001.rationale: It links low-latency model switching to keeping models resident in memory, but does not attribute that advantage to higher bandwidth to the accelerator than a host connection over PCIe provides.

sol-6.1.text: The big advantage is that you can keep many custom models resident in memory at the same time. If different users have models customized for their own data or applications, you don’t want to load a new model every time a request comes in. Moving those weights takes time and can become a bottleneck. With high-capacity memory, you can switch between models quickly and share the compute resources across them. That helps you deliver low latency without having to dedicate a separate system to every custom model.

r001.rationale: The response says keeping models resident avoids weight-loading delays and enables quick switching, but it does not attribute this to higher bandwidth than a host connection over PCIe.
